title: Stop guessing about the bathroom fan and check it properly
body:
The mirror still fogs for twenty minutes after a shower, which means the fan is moving far less air than it should.
- Pull the cover and clean the impeller — most likely cause, costs nothing
- Check the duct run in the loft for a crushed section or a disconnected joint
- Confirm the backdraught shutter at the outside vent actually opens
- Time the fogging before and after, so I know whether anything changed
- If it is still poor, price a quiet inline fan rather than another cheap axial one

shape: title contains =verbatim= markup (e.g. a file or tool name)
title: Collapse the scattered bread notes into one =sourdough.org= file
body: Timings, hydration and oven behaviour are currently spread over three notes, a photo of a napkin and my memory, so every bake starts by reconstructing the last one. One file, one table: flour blend, hydration, bulk time, room temperature, and a line on how the crumb came out. Room temperature is the variable I keep forgetting to write down and the one that explains most of the bad loaves.

title: Rebuild the daily piano hour around problem spots, not playthroughs
body:
The hour is there most days, which is not the problem. The problem is what happens inside it: I open the lid, play through the two pieces I can nearly play, hit the same four bars badly, and stop, feeling like I have practised. That is *rehearsal of my own mistakes*, and an hour a day of it is how you get reliably good at a wrong fingering.

Restructure it into three blocks and keep the blocks honest. Ten minutes of technique attached to no piece at all — scales, one arpeggio shape, hands separately — at a tempo slow enough that an error is not available to me. Then thirty minutes on a single problem spot, never more than two bars at a time, slow enough to be boring, and a click added only once the passage is already clean rather than as a way of forcing it clean. The final twenty minutes is the only part where playing the whole thing through is allowed, and even there the rule is to stop at the first stumble, mark the bar, and carry on instead of restarting. Restarting from the top is the habit that has made the opening of every piece I know much better than its middle.

What decides whether this survives a fortnight is the record, not the intention, so keep the record cheap: phone on the music desk, one take of the problem spot on Monday and one on Sunday, two lines in =practice-log.org= per session — bars worked, and the tempo at which they came out clean. Tempo-at-clean is the only number here that is genuinely a measurement; everything else is a feeling about how the session went, and my feelings about sessions are not well calibrated. Review the log at the end of each month and be willing to shelve a piece that has not moved in four weeks. Refs: [[obsidian:Piano practice]].
- On deliberate practice, and why time spent is the wrong thing to count
  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Practice_(learning_method)

shape: medium body ending with a bare URL alone on its last line
title: Plan one proper dark-sky night before the moon comes back
body:
The binoculars have been enough for the bright doubles, but I have never deliberately gone somewhere dark and stayed out past the point where my eyes adapt. Pick a new-moon weekend, check the forecast for transparency rather than just cloud cover, and go with a short list — four or five targets — instead of sweeping around hoping. A written list is what separates a good session from an hour of squinting.

https://www.timeanddate.com/astronomy/

shape: body with an org link that has a description: [[https://…][description]]
title: Learn to read the sidewall instead of trusting the tyre shop
body: Two of the tyres are from different makers and I could not tell you the load or speed rating on either, which is exactly the gap that gets exploited at replacement time. Write the full code, the DOT date and the tread depth for all four into the car note, then I can judge quotes myself and see which pair is aging out first. See [[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tire_code][the tyre code explained]] — the four-digit week-and-year stamp is the part I always miss.

shape: written entirely in Spanish, medium body
title: Fijar un turno estable en el banco de alimentos, no cuando me acuerdo
body: Aparecer un sábado suelto cada dos meses ayuda menos de lo que parece: el trabajo útil es el que se puede planificar, y para eso hacen falta manos previsibles. Comprometerme a un turno fijo, dos horas cada quince días, y avisar con antelación cuando no pueda ir. Preguntar también qué falta de verdad además de tiempo — casi siempre es alguien que sepa llevar el inventario o hacer una hoja de cálculo decente, y eso sí lo puedo hacer desde casa.

body: Лежит четыре тысячи файлов, смотреть их никто не будет, включая меня. Один снимок на день, остальное в холодное хранилище — и подписать места, пока ещё помню названия.

shape: title contains *bold* markup on the key word
title: Teach the group one *heavier* game properly, not badly twice
body: Every attempt so far has been a rules explanation at 21:00 on a weeknight, which is why the box goes back unfinished. Learn it alone first, play a solo dummy round, then teach it in ten minutes with the first turn open-handed. The failure mode is never the game, it is me reading rules aloud while four people wait.

shape: body uses /italic/ and ends with a [[obsidian:Note Title]] reference
title: Learn five autumn warblers well enough to stop writing "warbler sp."
body: In April I can separate them by song without thinking about it, and by late August the distinction is gone: everything moving in the hedge is a silent /Phylloscopus/ and the notebook gets another *warbler sp.* Pick the five that actually turn up on the river walk, learn one hard field mark for each rather than the whole plumage, and check myself against photographs before the sighting goes in. Chiffchaff against willow warbler is leg colour and primary projection once they have stopped singing, and that is the pair I get wrong. Refs: [[obsidian:River walk bird list]].

shape: body contains a small #+begin_src … #+end_src block (a shell command or a few lines of Python)
title: Get the statement PDFs into one folder with sane filenames
body:
Four banks, four naming conventions, and every year-end I spend an evening working out which file is which. Download everything once, then rename by date prefix so sorting alphabetically sorts chronologically. One pass with a loop, then never again:

#+begin_src sh
for f in *.pdf; do
  d=$(pdftotext "$f" - | grep -oEm1 '[0-9]{2}/[0-9]{2}/[0-9]{4}')
  echo "$f -> $d"
done
#+end_src

Run it printing only, check the extracted dates by eye, and do the actual move in a second pass. The retention question — how many years I keep and where the encrypted copy lives — is separate and I should not let it block this.

shape: two short paragraphs separated by a blank line, with a bare URL
title: Fix the hut-to-hut dates before the booking window opens
body:
Three nights in mountain huts, which makes the date the only real decision — beds go months ahead, trains do not. Book the huts first and fit the travel around whatever I get.

Then the unglamorous half: check which stages still hold snow that early, pick the two escape routes off the ridge, and write each day as ascent rather than distance, because kilometres are what fool me every time.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_du_Mont_Blanc

shape: title contains /italic/ markup; body uses =verbatim= for a measurement or part
title: Make a /proper/ crosscut sled before the next box project
body: Every mitre so far has been fought out with the stock fence, and the gaps in the last lid show it. Build the sled from the offcut of =18 mm= birch ply, fit runners to the slots with a few thousandths of slack, and square the fence with the five-cut method — one afternoon that pays for itself on the first joint.

title: Move the cat to measured meals and write down the numbers
body: Free-feeding means I have no idea what she actually eats, and the vet's weight note last visit was not encouraging. Weigh the daily ration, split it in two, and log weight monthly on the same scales. Details and the vet's target range go in [[obsidian:Cat health and feeding]].

title: Find out why the lane behind the church bends the way it does
body: It kinks twice for no reason the modern street layout explains, and both bends line up with the back edge of the gardens on the far side, which usually means something older is still setting the boundary. The obvious place to start is the tithe map and the earliest large-scale survey in the county record office, side by side with a current map, to see which lines survived and which were cut through. The library has a local history morning once a month where someone can point me at the right shelf faster than I will find it myself. Worth doing while the older neighbours are still around to ask, because half of what I want to know was never written down at all.
